claim: Recordings were conducted in 2 adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca Mulatta, M1, 13 kg; M2, 8 kg).
source: Anesthetized recordings were conducted in 2 adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca Mulatta, M1, 13 kg; M2, 8 kg).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the experimental subjects.

claim: The activity of V1 neurons was recorded using high-density, multi-contact Neuropixels probes (version 3A; IMEC Inc, Belgium).
source: The activity of V1 neurons was recorded in two anesthetized macaque monkeys (M1, M2) using high-density, multi-contact Neuropixels probes (version 3A; IMEC Inc, Belgium; Figure 1a; Methods).
evidence: Direct statement describing the recording methodology.

claim: Each Neuropixels probe consisted of 986 contacts (12 mm x 12 mm, 20 µm spacing) distributed across 10 mm, of which 384 contacts could be simultaneously selected for recording.
source: Each probe consisted of 986 contacts (12 mm x 12 mm, 20 µm spacing) distributed across 10 mm, of which 384 contacts could be simultaneously selected for recording.
evidence: Direct statement describing the technical specifications of the recording probe.

claim: The dense spacing between electrode contacts provided multiple measurements of the waveforms from individual neurons (mean = 4.52 measurements).
source: The dense spacing between electrode contacts provided multiple measurements of the waveforms from individual neurons (mean = 4.52 measurements) (Figure 1a and b)
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data about waveform measurements.

claim: In each of the 5 experimental sessions (3 in M1, 2 in M2), 115–221 simultaneously recorded neurons were measured.
source: In each of the 5 experimental sessions (3 in M1, 2 in M2), we measured the visual responses of 115–221 simultaneously recorded neurons to drifting gratings presented at varying orientations (total = 802 neurons).
evidence: Direct statement describing the number of neurons recorded across sessions.

claim: A total of 802 neurons were recorded across all sessions.
source: In each of the 5 experimental sessions (3 in M1, 2 in M2), we measured the visual responses of 115–221 simultaneously recorded neurons to drifting gratings presented at varying orientations (total = 802 neurons).
evidence: Direct statement providing the total number of neurons recorded.

claim: Neurons were highly orientation selective and exhibited both simple and complex cell properties.
source: As expected, neurons were highly orientation selective, and exhibited both simple and complex cell properties (De Valois et al., 1982; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Figure 1b).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature and reference to figure showing data.

claim: The ratio of simple to complex neurons was 1:2.4, with 236/802 neurons being simple and 566/802 neurons being complex.
source: The ratio of simple to complex neurons, respectively, was 1:2.4; 236/802 neurons were simple, and 566/802 neurons were complex.
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data about cell type distribution.

claim: CCGs were computed from the spike trains of 68,579 pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons (6,555–24,310 pairs/session).
source: CCGs were computed from the spike trains of 68,579 pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons (6,555–24,310 pairs/session, Methods).
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative data about the number of neuronal pairs analyzed.

claim: A CCG was considered significant only if its peak occurred within 10ms of zero time lag and if that peak was >7 standard deviations above the mean of the noise distribution.
source: In addition, as in previous studies, we considered a CCG significant only if its peak occurred within 10ms of zero time lag, and if that peak was >7 standard deviations above the mean of the noise distribution (Siegle et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct statement describing the statistical criteria used, supported by citation.

claim: A total of 10,246 significant CCGs were obtained from all recording sessions.
source: Using these criteria, a total of 10,246 significant CCGs were obtained from all recording sessions (Figure 1d), with each session yielding 755–3,022 significant CCGs.
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data and reference to figure.

claim: Each session yielded 755–3,022 significant CCGs.
source: Using these criteria, a total of 10,246 significant CCGs were obtained from all recording sessions (Figure 1d), with each session yielding 755–3,022 significant CCGs.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative data about CCGs per session.

claim: The synchrony of correlated spiking diminished several fold across neuronal pair distance.
source: The synchrony of correlated spiking diminished several fold across neuronal pair distance.
evidence: Direct statement describing the relationship between synchrony and distance.

claim: The relationship between peak lag and vertical distance could be fit with a linear function (r=0.42; p<10–5) in which the (absolute) peak lag increased at a rate of 1.3 ms / 500 µm of vertical distance.
source: This change could be fit with a linear function (r=0.42; p<10–5) in which the (absolute) peak lag increased at a rate of 1.3 ms / 500 µm of vertical distance.
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis results.

claim: Peak efficacy of the significant CCGs depended heavily on pair distance and could be fit with an exponential decay function (r=–0.34; p<10–5) in which the peak efficacy decreased by half within 154 µm.
source: This effect could be fit with an exponential decay function (r=–0.34; p<10–5) in which the peak efficacy decreased by half within 154 µm.
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis results.

claim: Both measures of functional interactions (peak lag and peak efficacy) depended heavily on the vertical distance separating neuronal pairs.
source: Thus, both measures of functional interactions depended heavily on the vertical distance separating neuronal pairs.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the findings about distance effects.

claim: The effects of vertical distance on both the synchrony and strength of CCGs were independent of whether neuronal pairs were located within the same or different cortical layers.
source: In addition, we confirmed that the effects of vertical distance on both the synchrony and strength of CCGs were independent of whether neuronal pairs were located within the same or different cortical layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to supplementary figure showing the analysis.

claim: Across the total number of neuronal pairs (N=68,579), the mean rori was 0.25.
source: Across the total number of neuronal pairs (N=68,579), the mean rori was 0.25.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative data about signal correlations.

claim: For the significantly correlated neuronal pairs, the mean rori was 0.33.
source: For the significantly correlated neuronal pairs, the mean rori was 0.33.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative data about signal correlations in significant pairs.

claim: Both the peak lag and peak efficacy of CCGs for significantly correlated neuronal pairs varied monotonically with tuning similarity across the range of signal correlations.
source: Overall, we found that both the peak lag and peak efficacy of CCGs for significantly correlated neuronal pairs varied monotonically with tuning similarity across the range of signal correlations (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Neuronal pairs with the highest signal correlations exhibited half the peak lags and twice the peak efficacies of uncorrelated pairs.
source: Neuronal pairs with the highest signal correlations exhibited half the peak lags and twice the peak efficacies of uncorrelated pairs.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative comparison of correlated vs uncorrelated pairs.

claim: The differences in peak lags of distance-matched CCGs were negatively correlated with signal correlation.
source: Indeed, we found that the differences in peak lags of distance-matched CCGs were negatively correlated with signal correlation (Figure 3e)
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing the analysis.

claim: The differences in peak efficacies of distance-matched CCGs were positively correlated with signal correlation.
source: and the differences in peak efficacies of distance-matched CCGs were positively correlated with signal correlation (Figure 3f).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing the analysis.

claim: Signal correlations within the column predicted both the synchrony and strength of functional interactions independent of vertical pair distance.
source: These results indicate that signal correlations within the column predicted both the synchrony and strength of functional interactions independent of vertical pair distance.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the findings from distance-matched analysis.

claim: The vertical distance between neurons and their orientation signal correlations exhibit distinct, but overlapping, effects on the timing and strength of functional interactions within a single cortical column.
source: Nonetheless, the distance-matched correlations (Figure 3e–f) were smaller than their corresponding unmatched correlations (Figure 3c–d), suggesting that the vertical distance between neurons and their orientation signal correlations exhibit distinct, but overlapping, effects on the timing and strength of functional interactions within a single cortical column.
evidence: Statement based on comparison of statistical results with references to figures.

claim: For CCG peak lag, the coefficient of pair distance was nearly three times the coefficient of signal correlation.
source: Thus, for CCG peak lag, the coefficient of pair distance was nearly three times the coefficient of signal correlation.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing regression coefficient comparison.

claim: For CCG peak efficacy, the coefficient of signal correlation was nearly twice that of pair distance.
source: In contrast, for CCG peak efficacy, the coefficient of signal correlation was nearly twice that of pair distance.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing regression coefficient comparison.

claim: Four distinct classes of functional interactions were identified through clustering analysis.
source: From this, we selected four as the optimal number of clusters given that silhouette score peaked ~3–4 clusters, and 4 clusters explained more variance than 3.
evidence: Direct statement describing the clustering results and rationale for selecting four clusters.

claim: Synchronous classes exhibited higher average peak efficacies than asynchronous classes (median peak efficacy: Ssync 0.021, Bsync 0.020, Fasync 0.015, Rasync 0.014).
source: Aside from clear differences in peak lags between subsets of the putative classes (e.g. synchronous vs. asynchronous), CCGs of different classes also differed in their peak efficacies; synchronous classes exhibited higher average peak efficacies than asynchronous classes (median peak efficacy: Ssync 0.021, Bsync 0.020, Fasync 0.015, Rasync 0.014).
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data comparing peak efficacies across classes.

claim: Vertical pair distances were larger and orientation signal correlations were smaller in asynchronous (Fasync and Rasync) than in synchronous (Ssync and Bsync) classes.
source: Indeed, we found that vertical pair distances were larger and orientation signal correlations were smaller in asynchronous (Fasync and Rasync) than in synchronous (Ssync and Bsync) classes (Figure 5a–b) (significant pairwise comparisons: p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical results and reference to figures.

claim: Bsync pairs were separated by greater vertical distances than Ssync ones (p<10–5).
source: For example, we found that in spite of exhibiting similar CCG peak lags, Bsync pairs were separated by greater vertical distances than Ssync ones (Figure 5a; p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical result and reference to figure.

claim: Bsync pairs exhibited higher signal correlations than Ssync pairs (p<10–5).
source: Furthermore, in spite of being separated by a greater cortical distance, Bsync pairs exhibited higher signal correlations than Ssync pairs (Figure 5b; p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical result and reference to figure.

claim: Different classes of functional interactions were differentially distributed across V1 layers such that one or more of the identified classes was often overrepresented among functional interactions within particular layers (p<10–5).
source: Indeed, we found that different classes were differentially distributed across V1 layers such that one or more of the identified classes was often overrepresented among functional interactions within particular layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical result and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Most of the asynchronous pairs were composed of neurons from different layers, while most of the synchronous pairs, particularly the Ssync ones, were composed of neurons from the same layer.
source: We found that most of the asynchronous pairs were composed of neurons from different layers, while most of the synchronous pairs, particularly the Ssync ones, were composed of neurons from the same layer (Figure 5c) (within vs between proportion: Ssync [0.65 vs 0.35], Bsync [0.52 vs 0.48], F [0.29 vs 0.71], R [0.27 vs 0.73], one proportion z-test: Ssync, F, R: P<10–5; Bsync: p=0.022).
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data, statistical results, and reference to figure.

claim: Cortical layer had an independent effect of distance on CCG class assignment among nearby (~200 μm) pairs of neurons.
source: Nonetheless, we found that cortical layer had an independent effect of distance on CCG class assignment among nearby (~200 μm) pairs of neurons.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the results of logistic regression analysis.

claim: Among the significant CCGs, a majority were comprised of pairs of complex cells (S/S=5.2%, C/C=63%; S/C=31.8%; one-proportion z-test: p<10–5).
source: Among the significant CCGs, a majority were comprised of pairs of complex cells (S/S=5.2%, C/C=63%; S/C=31.8%; one-proportion z-test: p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data and statistical result.

claim: Among significantly correlated neuronal pairs composed of a simple cell as the reference neuron and a complex cell as the target neuron, the proportion of forward (Fasync) CCGs was larger than the reverse (Rasync) class (p<10–5).
source: We found that the proportion of forward (Fasync) CCGs was larger than the reverse (Rasync) class (p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical result about simple-complex cell interactions.

claim: For the 4cα-4cα, 4cβ-4cβ, and 6–6 pairings, Ssync CCGs were observed much more frequently than other CCG classes (chi-squared test; 4cα-4cα, 4cβ-4cβ: P<10–5, 6–6: P<10–2).
source: We found that for the 4cα-4cα, 4cβ-4cβ, and 6–6 pairings, Ssync CCGs were observed much more frequently than other CCG classes (Figure 6b) (chi-squared test; 4cα-4cα, 4cβ-4cβ: P<10–5, 6–6: P<10–2).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical results and reference to figure.

claim: The Fasync class was significantly overrepresented in 6–4cα and 6-4cβ pairs where the layer 6 neuron was the reference neuron (6–4cα: p<10–5, 6-4cβ: p<10–3).
source: Indeed, in addition to observing that Ssync CCGs were poorly represented, we found that the Fasync class was significantly overrepresented in these pairs (Figure 6d) (6–4cα: p<10–5, 6-4cβ: p<10–3).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical results and reference to figure.

claim: The forward (Fasync) class was overrepresented among functional interactions from layers 6, 5, 4cβ, 4cα, and 4A/B to layer 2/3 (chi-squared test; 6: p<10–5; 5: p<10–5; 4cβ: p<10–3; 4cα: p<10–2; 4A/B: p<10–5).
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that the forward (Fasync) class was overrepresented among functional interactions from layers 6, 5, 4cβ, 4cα, and 4A/B to layer 2/3 (Figure 7b) (chi-squared test; 6: p<10–5; 5: p<10–5; 4cβ: p<10–3; 4cα: p<10–2; 4A/B: p<10–5).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical results and reference to figure.

claim: Within layer 2/3, the Ssync and Bsync CCGs were overrepresented among functional interactions (chi-squared test: p<10–4).
source: Within layer 2/3, the Ssync and Bsync CCGs were overrepresented among functional interactions (Figure 7c) (chi-squared test: p<10–4)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical result and reference to figure.

claim: There was an equal representation of Ssync and Bsync CCGs among 2/3-2/3 pairings.
source: and there was an equal representation of Ssync and Bsync CCGs among 2/3-2/3 pairings.
evidence: Direct statement about the distribution of CCG classes within layer 2/3.

claim: Using high-density recordings from single neocortical columns of macaque V1, 1000s of functionally interacting neuronal pairs were identified using established crosscorrelation approaches.
source: Using high-density recordings from single neocortical columns of macaque V1, we identified 1000s of functionally interacting neuronal pairs using established crosscorrelation approaches.
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section summarizing the main finding.

claim: The results demonstrate clear and systematic variations in the synchrony and strength of functional interactions within single V1 columns.
source: The results demonstrate clear and systematic variations in the synchrony and strength of functional interactions within single V1 columns.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the main findings.

claim: The functional interactions between pairs of V1 neurons depended heavily on their vertical distance within the column, with both the peak lag and peak efficacy of CCGs changing dramatically within only a few hundred micrometers of vertical distance.
source: Notably, we observed that in spite of residing within the same column, the functional interactions between pairs of V1 neurons depended heavily on their vertical distance within the column; both the peak lag and peak efficacy of CCGs between neuronal pairs changed dramatically within only a few hundred micrometers of vertical distance within the column.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the findings about distance effects.

claim: The synchrony and strength of CCGs also depended on laminar location and the similarity of orientation tuning between neuronal pairs.
source: In addition, we found that the synchrony and strength of CCGs also depended on laminar location and the similarity of orientation tuning between neuronal pairs.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing findings about laminar and tuning effects.

claim: Distinct classes of functional interactions exhibited different distributions across defined laminar compartments, and those differences were consistent with known and/or expected properties of V1 cortical circuitry.
source: Those distinct classes exhibited different distributions across defined laminar compartments, and those differences were consistent with known and/or expected properties of V1 cortical circuitry.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the findings about class distributions and their consistency with known circuitry.

claim: Evidence from previous studies suggests that correlations are greatest for pairs of neurons located within the same column, and diminish with greater columnar distance.
source: Evidence from these studies suggest that correlations are greatest for pairs of neurons located within the same column, and diminish with greater columnar distance.
evidence: Statement summarizing findings from prior literature.

claim: The observed rate of asynchronous classes identified in the data is consistent with estimates of the connection probability among V1 neurons obtained in multi-patch, slice recordings.
source: Thus, in spite of the inherent arbitrariness of the statistical criteria employed in identifying significant CCGs, the observed proportion of asynchronous interactions among pairs in our data appears largely consistent with previous estimates.
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior literature estimates.

claim: Using the criterion from Hembrook-Short et al., 2019 that required CCG peaks be sharp and narrow (<5ms) to be considered monosynaptic, 86% of the asynchronous CCGs were categorized as consistent with monosynaptic connections.
source: As a means of comparing the criteria used here to those of prior studies in monkey V1, we applied one criterion used in Hembrook-Short et al., 2019 to our data, which required that CCG peaks be sharp and narrow (<5ms) to be considered monosynaptic. Using this criterion, we found that 86% of our asynchronous CCGs were categorized as consistent with monosynaptic connections.
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative result from applying a criterion from prior literature.

claim: The frequency of excitatory CCGs in the dataset was considerably higher than that of inhibitory CCGs.
source: As in previous studies, the frequency of excitatory CCGs in our dataset was considerably higher than that of inhibitory CCGs (Aertsen and Gerstein, 1985; Hembrook-Short et al., 2019; Table 2).
evidence: Direct statement with citations and reference to table showing the data.

claim: 136 CCGs had troughs that were more than 7 SD below noise whereas 10,246 CCGs had peaks that were more than 7 SD above noise.
source: 136 CCGs had troughs that were more than 7 SD below noise whereas 10,246 CCGs had peaks that were more than 7 SD above noise.
evidence: Direct statement from Table 2 caption providing quantitative data.

claim: The observed proportion of asynchronous interactions among pairs (~9% of total pairs tested) is consistent with estimates of synaptic connectivity in 5–12% of excitatory neurons in mouse/rat V1 from multi-patch, slice recordings.
source: For example, recent studies identified synaptic connectivity in 5–12% of excitatory neurons in mouse/rat V1 (Cadwell et al., 2020; Song et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior literature with citations.

claim: Probes were inserted into the lateral operculum of V1 with the aid of a surgical microscope at angles nearly perpendicular to the cortical surface.
source: Probes were inserted into the lateral operculum of V1 with the aid of a surgical microscope at angles nearly perpendicular to the cortical surface.
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: Receptive field eccentricities were ~4–6° (M1) and ~6–10° (M2).
source: RF eccentricities were ~4–6° (M1) and ~6–10° (M2).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section providing quantitative data about receptive fields.

claim: Gratings drifted in 36 different directions between 0–360° in 10° steps in a pseudorandom order.
source: Gratings drifted in 36 different directions between 0–360° in 10° steps in a pseudorandom order.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the stimulus parameters.

claim: Four spatial frequencies (0.5, 1, 2, 4 cycle/deg.) were tested and optimal SFs were determined offline to categorize V1 neurons into simple or complex cell.
source: Four spatial frequencies (0.5, 1, 2, 4 cycle/deg.) were tested and optimal SFs were determined offline to categorize V1 neurons into simple or complex cell.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: The stimulus in each condition was presented for 1 second and repeated 5 or 10 times.
source: The stimulus in each condition was presented for 1 second and repeated 5 or 10 times.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the stimulus presentation.

claim: Raw spike-band data was sampled and recorded at 30 kHz.
source: Raw spike-band data was sampled and recorded at 30 kHz.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the data acquisition.

claim: Spike-sorting was carried out with Kilosort2.
source: Spike-sorting was carried out with Kilosort2 (https://github.com/MouseLand/Kilosort; Pachitariu et al., 2022) to find spike times and assign each spike to different units.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the spike sorting procedure.

claim: Only neurons with a minimum firing rate of 3 spikes/s were included in the study.
source: Moreover, only neurons with a minimum firing rate of 3 spikes/s were included in the study.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the inclusion criteria.

claim: Out of the total 68,579 pairs of neurons included in this study, only 7 pairs shared more than 20% overlapping spikes.
source: Out of the total 68,579 pairs of neurons included in this current study, we found that only 7 pairs shared more than 20% overlapping spikes.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section providing quantitative data about potential double-counting.

claim: Simple cells were defined as cells with modulation ratio larger than 1, and complex cells have modulation ratios smaller than 1.
source: Simple cells were defined as cells with modulation ratio larger than 1, and complex cells have modulation ratios smaller than 1 (De Valois et al., 1982; Skottun et al., 1991).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the classification criteria with citations.

claim: A 25 ms jitter window was chosen for jitter correction based on previous studies.
source: Here, a 25 ms jitter window was chosen based on previous studies (Jia et al., 2013; Siegle et al., 2021; Zandvakili and Kohn, 2015).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the methodological choice with citations.

claim: t-SNE was used instead of PCA for dimensionality reduction because it is more robust to outliers since it captures neighbor relationships in the input space.
source: t-SNE was used instead of principal component analysis (PCA) because it is more robust to outliers since it captures neighbor relationships in the input space.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section explaining the rationale for methodological choice.

claim: More than 99% (5067/5122) of the distance-matched pairs had a difference in cortical distance of less than 2 µm.
source: More than 99% (5067/5122) of the distance-matched pairs had a difference in cortical distance of less than 2 µm.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section providing quantitative data about the distance-matching procedure.

claim: The columnar organization of the mammalian neocortex and its distinctly layered structure within different cortical domains are both widely appreciated.
source: The columnar organization of the mammalian neocortex (Lorente de No, 1938; Mountcastle, 1957) and its distinctly layered structure within different cortical domains are both widely appreciated (Reviewed in DeFelipe et al., 2012; Horton and Adams, 2005; Mountcastle, 1997).
evidence: Statement about established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Several key principles of cortical circuitry, including constituent cell types, input-output organization and local microcircuit motifs have emerged in recent years.
source: In addition, several key principles of cortical circuitry, including constituent cell types (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Jiang et al., 2015; Kätzel et al., 2011; Markram et al., 2004; Network, 2021; Packer and Yuste, 2011; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005), input-output organization (Callaway, 1998; Douglas and Martin, 2004; Lefort et al., 2009; Muñoz-Castañeda et al., 2021; Thomson and Bannister, 2003; Weiler et al., 2008) and local microcircuit motifs (Avermann et al., 2012; Frandolig et al., 2019; Karnani et al., 2016; Obermayer et al., 2018; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013) have emerged in recent years.
evidence: Statement about established knowledge with extensive citations.

claim: Such principles may turn out to generalize not only across neocortical areas, but also across species.
source: Although it remains to be determined, such principles may turn out to generalize not only across neocortical areas, but also across species (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Karten, 2015; Stacho et al., 2020) (see also Campagnola et al., 2022; Wildenberg et al., 2021).
evidence: Speculative statement with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Mapping complete cortical microcircuits within even a single cortical area remains a tremendous challenge.
source: Yet, mapping complete cortical microcircuits within even a single cortical area remains a tremendous challenge (Adesnik and Naka, 2018).
evidence: Statement about the current state of the field with citation.

claim: Recent advances in recording technology have facilitated the development of large-scale, high-density micro-electrode arrays resulting in a substantial increment (>10x) in the number of neurons that can be studied simultaneously within a localized area of neural tissue.
source: Recent advances in recording technology have facilitated the development of large-scale, high-density micro-electrode arrays resulting in a substantial increment (>10x) in the number of neurons that can be studied simultaneously within a localized area of neural tissue.
evidence: Statement about technological advances.

claim: The Neuropixels probe consists of a high-channel count Si shank with continuous, dense, programmable recording sites (~1000/cm).
source: A prime example is the recent development of the Neuropixels probe (IMEC, Inc), which consists of a high-channel count Si shank with continuous, dense, programmable recording sites (~1000/cm).
evidence: Direct statement describing the technical specifications of the probe.

claim: Numerous recent studies have demonstrated the advantages of Neuropixels probes, such as their use in recording large neuronal populations within deep structures where optical approaches cannot be deployed.
source: Numerous recent studies have demonstrated the advantages of such probes, such as their use in recording large neuronal populations within deep structures where optical approaches cannot be deployed (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about prior work with citations.

claim: The high-density capacity of Neuropixels probes dramatically increases the quantity of single neurons that can be obtained within a localized area of neural tissue, thus making them well-suited for investigations of local neuronal circuitry.
source: In addition, the high-density capacity of such probes dramatically increases the quantity of single neurons that can be obtained within a localized area of neural tissue (Siegle et al., 2021), thus making them well-suited for investigations of local neuronal circuitry.
evidence: Statement about the advantages of the technology with citation.

claim: Only a few electrophysiological studies of the primate brain using Neuropixels probes have been carried out thus far.
source: However, only a few electrophysiological studies of the primate brain using such probes have been carried out thus far (Hesse and Tsao, 2020; Paulk et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022; Trautmann et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about the current state of the field with citations.

claim: Many studies have leveraged the covariation in spiking activity between simultaneously recorded neurons to elucidate underlying neural mechanisms in the primate brain with some success, particularly within the visual system.
source: To date, many studies have leveraged the covariation in spiking activity between simultaneously recorded neurons to elucidate underlying neural mechanisms in the primate brain with some success, particularly within the visual system (Briggs et al., 2013; Chu et al., 2014; Hansen et al., 2012; Hembrook-Short et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2013; Kohn and Smith, 2005; Koren et al., 2020; Krüger and Aiple, 1988; Maldonado et al., 2000; Smith and Kohn, 2008; Zandvakili and Kohn, 2015).
evidence: Statement about prior work with extensive citations.

claim: Temporally precise correlations in spiking activity have provided a unique means of assessing interactions among neurons in both local and distributed networks.
source: In particular, temporally precise correlations in spiking activity have provided a unique means of assessing interactions among neurons in both local and distributed networks (Aertsen and Gerstein, 1985; Aertsen et al., 1989; Diba et al., 2014; Moore et al., 1970; Nelson et al., 1992; Nowak et al., 1999; Perkel et al., 1967; Siegle et al., 2021)
evidence: Statement about established methodology with citations.

claim: Identification of functional interactions has played an important part in understanding neural circuits in the mammalian visual system.
source: and identification of such interactions has played an important part in understanding neural circuits in the mammalian visual system (Alonso and Martinez, 1998; Alonso et al., 1996; Alonso et al., 2001; Baker and Bair, 2012; Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Das and Gilbert, 1999; Denman and Contreras, 2014; Michalski et al., 1983; Nelson et al., 1992; Reid and Alonso, 1995; Schwarz and Bolz, 1991; Senzai et al., 2019; Siegle et al., 2021; Toyama et al., 1981a; Ts'o et al., 1986; Usrey et al., 1998; Usrey et al., 1999).
evidence: Statement about the importance of the approach with extensive citations.

claim: The extent of circuit-level details addressable with crosscorrelation is greatly limited by the low incidences of simultaneous recordings from connected neurons when using conventional extracellular recording techniques.
source: However, the extent of circuit-level details addressable with crosscorrelation is greatly limited by the low incidences of simultaneous recordings from connected neurons when using conventional extracellular recording techniques (e.g. Alonso et al., 2001; Hembrook-Short et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 1992; Ts'o et al., 1986).
evidence: Statement about limitations of conventional approaches with citations.

claim: The use of high channel-count probes should substantially mitigate the limitation of low incidences of simultaneous recordings from connected neurons by virtue of the large increment in recording yield.
source: The use of high channel-count probes should substantially mitigate that limitation by virtue of the large increment in recording yield.
evidence: Statement about the expected advantage of the technology.

claim: The high-density of recordings should further increase the incidence of identifiable correlated neuronal activity by virtue of the proximity of recorded cells.
source: Moreover, the high-density of recordings should further increase the incidence of identifiable correlated neuronal activity by virtue of the proximity of recorded cells.
evidence: Statement about the expected advantage of the technology.

claim: Crosscorrelation assesses the statistical dependencies between spike trains of two or more neurons and has long played an important role in estimating how ensembles of neurons interact with one another.
source: Crosscorrelation assesses the statistical dependencies between spike trains of two or more neurons and has long played an important role in estimating how ensembles of neurons interact with one another (Casile et al., 2021; Okatan et al., 2005; Perkel et al., 1967).
evidence: Statement about the methodology with citations.

claim: Crosscorrelation is the most widely used method for assessing statistical dependencies between spike trains, perhaps due to its simplicity.
source: Although a number of different analyses have been employed (Casile et al., 2021; Keeley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2019), crosscorrelation is the most widely used, perhaps due to its simplicity.
evidence: Statement about the prevalence of the method with citations.

claim: Significant crosscorrelations are broadly interpreted as identifying 'functional connections' or 'functional interactions' among neurons.
source: Significant crosscorrelations are broadly interpreted as identifying 'functional connections' (Aertsen and Gerstein, 1985; Dann et al., 2016; Denman and Contreras, 2014; Menz and Freeman, 2004; Schwarz and Bolz, 1991) or 'functional interactions' among neurons (Gochin et al., 1991; Ostojic et al., 2009)
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of crosscorrelations with citations.

claim: Functional interactions are interpreted as reflecting one of myriad putative circuit arrangements among neuronal pairs, arrangements which include direct monosynaptic connections or neurons with common input.
source: These functional interactions are interpreted as reflecting one of myriad putative circuit arrangements among neuronal pairs (Aertsen and Gerstein, 1985; Melssen and Epping, 1987; Moore et al., 1970; Ostojic et al., 2009), arrangements which include direct monosynaptic connections (Alonso and Martinez, 1998; English et al., 2017; Reid and Alonso, 1995) or neurons with common input (Constantinidis et al., 2001; Das and Gilbert, 1999; Denman and Contreras, 2014; Michalski et al., 1983; Ts'o et al., 1986; Türker and Powers, 2001)
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of functional interactions with extensive citations.

claim: ~15% (10,246/68,579) of neuronal pairs within columns of macaque V1 exhibited significant functional interactions.
source: Using statistical criteria employed in a recent study of mouse visual cortex (Siegle et al., 2021), we found that ~15% (10,246/68,579) of neuronal pairs within columns of macaque V1 exhibited significant functional interactions.
evidence: Direct statement with quantitative data and citation.

claim: The proportion of significant pairs (~15%) is within the range observed in previous studies in macaque V1.
source: The proportion of significant pairs is within the range observed in previous studies in macaque V1 (Chu et al., 2014; Hembrook-Short et al., 2019; Kohn and Smith, 2005; Smith and Kohn, 2008).
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior literature with citations.

claim: The proportion of significant pairs is also similar to previous CCG measurements made in the cat and mouse V1.
source: In addition, the proportion of significant pairs is also similar to previous CCG measurements made in the cat (Alonso and Martinez, 1998) and mouse V1 (Denman and Contreras, 2014; Siegle et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior literature with citations.

claim: The statistical interdependence of spike trains is not necessarily an indicator of synaptic connectivity among neurons.
source: In addition, it has long been understood that the statistical interdependence of spike trains is not necessarily an indicator of synaptic connectivity among neurons (Ostojic et al., 2009; Perkel et al., 1967).
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of spike train correlations with citations.

claim: Spike crosscorrelations are in no way a substitute for more direct measurements of synaptic connectivity, for example multi-patch recordings or electron microscopy.
source: Indeed, spike crosscorrelations are in no way a substitute for more direct measurements of synaptic connectivity, for example multi-patch recordings (Cadwell et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2015; Song et al., 2005) or electron microscopy (Bock et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about the limitations of the method with citations.

claim: Only a subset of the identified CCG classes are consistent with, although not necessarily indicative of, monosynaptically connected neuronal pairs.
source: Notably, only a subset of the identified CCG classes here are consistent with, although not necessarily indicative of, monosynaptically connected neuronal pairs.
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of CCG classes.

claim: Pairs with non-zero time lags, such as the asynchronous (Fasync and Rasync) classes, are those most likely to be monosynaptically connected.
source: Specifically, pairs with non-zero time lags, such as the asynchronous (Fasync and Rasync) classes we describe are those most likely to be monosynaptically connected.
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of asynchronous CCG classes.

claim: The asynchronous class amounted to ~9% of the total pairs tested.
source: In our data, the asynchronous class amounted to ~9% of the total pairs tested.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative data.

claim: The synchronous classes, particularly the Ssync class, which are more likely to reflect pairs with common input, amounted to ~6% of the total pairs tested.
source: In contrast, the synchronous classes, particularly the Ssync class, which are more likely to reflect pairs with common input (Ostojic et al., 2009; Perkel et al., 1967), amounted to ~6% of the total pairs tested.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative data with citations about interpretation.

claim: There exists little or no ground-truth measurements of the rate of synaptic connectivity, or common input, between neurons within single V1 columns in any species.
source: Unfortunately, there exists little or no ground-truth measurements of the rate of synaptic connectivity, or common input, between neurons within single V1 columns in any species, though such measurements may be imminent (https://www.microns-explorer.org/).
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Evidence that spiking correlations and synchrony decline with horizontal cortical distance within V1 has been shown in cats, monkeys, and mice.
source: Evidence that spiking correlations and synchrony decline with horizontal cortical distance within V1 has been shown in cats (Das and Gilbert, 1999; Gray et al., 1989; Hata et al., 1991) (but see Samonds et al., 2006; Schwarz and Bolz, 1991), monkeys (Chu et al., 2014; Krüger and Aiple, 1988; Maldonado et al., 2000; Smith and Kohn, 2008), and in mice (Denman and Contreras, 2014).
evidence: Statement summarizing prior literature with extensive citations.

claim: Very few studies have examined crosscorrelations among pairs of neurons within a single column, where the feedforward input is largely shared.
source: Very few studies have examined crosscorrelations among pairs of neurons within a single column, where the feedforward input is largely shared (e.g. DeAngelis et al., 1999).
evidence: Statement about the current state of the field with citation.

claim: Longer timescale, spike count ('noise'), correlations have been shown to be layer dependent within macaque V1 where weaker correlations occur in layer 4.
source: Longer timescale, spike count ('noise'), correlations, which have been widely assessed in studies of primate visual cortex (Averbeck et al., 2006) have been shown to be layer dependent within macaque V1 where weaker correlations occur in layer 4 (Hansen et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: No evidence that spike count correlations depend on distance independent of layer was observed in macaque V1.
source: However, no evidence that such correlations depend on distance independent of layer was observed.
evidence: Statement about the absence of a finding in prior work.

claim: Measurement of crosscorrelations in earlier studies of V1 columns in cat suggest that functional interactions are restricted to local regions across cortical depths.
source: In contrast, measurement of crosscorrelations in earlier studies of V1 columns in cat indeed suggest that functional interactions are restricted to local regions across cortical depths (Toyama et al., 1981b).
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citation.

claim: Within rat auditory cortex, functional interactions diminish dramatically within ~300 µm of vertical columnar distance.
source: Within rat auditory cortex, functional interactions diminish dramatically within ~300 µm of vertical columnar distance (Atencio and Schreiner, 2013), similar to what is observed in rat somatosensory cortex (Khateb et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: A dependence of interactions on vertical distance is supported by evidence from multiple whole-cell recordings in mouse visual cortex which demonstrates that connection probability decreases sharply within a distance of 250 µm.
source: A dependence of interactions on vertical distance is further supported by evidence from multiple whole-cell recordings in mouse visual cortex which demonstrates that connection probability decreases sharply within a distance of 250 µm (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citation.

claim: The observation that the peak efficacy of CCGs was greatly diminished within <200 µm within macaque V1 is consistent with estimates from other sensory cortices and species.
source: Our observation that the peak efficacy of CCGs was greatly diminished within <200 µm within macaque V1 is thus consistent with estimates from other sensory cortices and species.
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior literature.

claim: Many previous studies have reported an effect of tuning similarity on functional interactions, yet most of these studies focused on interactions between pairs of neurons in different cortical columns.
source: Many previous studies have reported an effect of tuning similarity on functional interactions, yet most of these studies focused on interactions between pairs of neurons in different cortical columns.
evidence: Statement about prior work.

claim: Evidence from horizontal array recordings in macaque V1 suggests that pairs of neurons selective for similar orientations, or color and luminance, tend to exhibit stronger functional interactions compared to pairs with dissimilar tuning.
source: Evidence from horizontal array recordings in macaque V1 suggests that pairs of neurons selective for similar orientations (Chu et al., 2014; Kohn and Smith, 2005; Smith and Kohn, 2008), or color and luminance (Chu et al., 2014) tend to exhibit stronger functional interactions compared to pairs with dissimilar tuning, perhaps reflecting the functional specificity of horizontal connections (Gilbert and Wiesel, 1989).
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: One study found that the strength of functional interactions between neuronal pairs with the highest orientation signal correlations was nearly twice that of uncorrelated pairs.
source: For example, one study found that the strength of functional interactions between neuronal pairs with the highest orientation signal correlations was nearly twice that of uncorrelated pairs (Smith and Kohn, 2008).
evidence: Statement about a specific prior finding with citation.

claim: In contrast to comparisons across columns where tuning similarity appears to be the primary factor, within single columns, vertical distance and orientation tuning similarity exerted distinct effects on the synchrony and strength of functional interactions.
source: In addition, in contrast to comparisons across columns where tuning similarity appears to be the primary factor (Chu et al., 2014), we found that within single columns, vertical distance and orientation tuning similarity exerted distinct effects on the synchrony and strength of functional interactions.
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior work with citation.

claim: The choice of three classes was almost as valid as that of four in the clustering procedure.
source: Indeed, the choice of three classes was almost as valid as that of four in the clustering procedure (Figure 4).
evidence: Statement about the clustering analysis with reference to figure.

claim: Given the clear evidence of two asynchronous classes, and the differential distributions of broadly and sharply synchronous pairs across cortical layers, the choice of only three classes of CCGs seems less parsimonious than four.
source: Yet, given the clear evidence of two asynchronous classes, and the differential distributions of broadly and sharply synchronous pairs across cortical layers, the choice of only three classes of CCGs seems less parsimonious than four.
evidence: Statement providing reasoning for the choice of four clusters.

claim: Additional distinct classes of CCGs might be present, but significantly less frequent or weaker than the other four.
source: Although there appeared to be less evidence for the existence of five or more classes of functional interactions, that possibility cannot be ruled out either. For example, additional distinct classes of CCGs might be present, but significantly less frequent or weaker than the other four.

claim: The selection criteria excluded CCGs with significant inhibitory peaks given their low incidence.
source: Indeed, given their low incidence, our selection criteria already excluded CCGs with significant inhibitory peaks.

claim: The pattern of differential distributions of the putative classes of CCGs across the column and across functional pairs of neurons was largely consistent with known properties of V1 microcircuitry.
source: Thus, overall, we found that the pattern of differential distributions of the putative classes of CCGs across the column and across functional pairs of neurons was largely consistent with known properties of V1 microcircuitry.
evidence: Statement summarizing the findings and their consistency with prior knowledge.

claim: The relative instances of different types of crosscorrelations observed among large populations of neuronal pairs may provide a means of constraining models of cortical microcircuits.
source: We found that the relative instances of different types of crosscorrelations observed among large populations of neuronal pairs may provide a means of constraining models of cortical microcircuits.

source: This approach could prove particularly valuable in less experimentally tractable model systems such as nonhuman primates, or perhaps even in the human brain, where direct interrogation of microcircuits is difficult or not yet possible.

claim: Future studies should be able to compare local interactions across different putative cell types estimated from their spike waveforms and/or spiking patterns.

source: In the macaque brain, dLGN magnocellular and parvocellular axons primarily project to V1 layers 4cα and 4cβ, respectively, along with inputs that terminate in layer 6 (reviewed in Briggs and Usrey, 2011; Lund, 1988; Merigan and Maunsell, 1993; Nassi and Callaway, 2009; Figure 6a).
